To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) liberal democracy mitigates political violence for groups with compatible identities and facilitates it for those with incompatible ones; 2) this is due to an internal contradiction of liberal democracy, which, while claiming to accommodate diverse groups and hence provide security to all, this accommodation does extend to its core values about ‘the good society’; and 3) this paradox is a result of liberal democracy's identity construction as a political community, which is based on a ‘we-they’ dichotomy
liberal democracy can facilitate as well as mitigate recourse to political (violent) action.
the relationship between liberal democracy and political violence is paradoxical.

how the identity security of a group can be threatened by a liberal democratic framework.
the paradox of identity security in liberal democracy. It is a paradox which has been neglected and which is important to address as
the paradox that liberal democracy, in accommodating group identity, can facilitate the very recourse to political violence it seeks to mitigate.

liberal democracy mitigatesthe use of political violence for those who share its identity, but facilitates it for those who do not.

liberal democracy can mitigate and facilitate recourse to political violence, but the conditions under which this occurs are contingent on the nature of the group identities that encounter the liberal democratic framework.
liberal democracy mitigated recourse to political violence in Spain for the Basques, while it facilitated it in the USA for the American Indians.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the paradox of identity security in liberal democracy stems from the tension between its core principles and the need to provide security to groups with diverse identities.
the liberal democratic framework can mitigate recourse to violence for those groups which share the same core values and principles.

, as a consequence of the internal contradiction of liberal democracy, the ‘societal security dilemma’ can be resolved in a way that mitigates or facilitates recourse to political violence, depending on whether the identity of ‘Other’ is compatible or incompatible with its core liberal principles.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the liberal democratic framework does not necessarily provide identity security for those who do not share the liberal identity, but rather it can facilitate their recourse to political violence, as the case of ETA illustrates.
, if liberal democratic institutions are to mitigate recourse to political, then they need to accommodate and provide security for the diverse identities that constitute them.
liberal democracy can be both a facilitator of and a mitigator against political violence, depending upon how the groups within it construct their identities.
